name: insights
description: Tell a founder's story or principle through their own words. Short paragraphs, lots of line breaks, direct quotes mixed with sharp narrative. The hook is a bold statement or specific claim. Build the story beat by beat. End with a punchy closing line. NOT analysis — it's storytelling.
examples:
Coinbase co-founder, Brian Armstrong, on why the best co-founder disagreements are resolved using a number, not a title:

"It would be a bad move for me to say every time, well I'm the CEO, so I'm making the final call. That's a good recipe to just piss off other people who are working with you."

Brian and his co-founder agree on 90-95% of decisions. For the 5%, they needed something better than hierarchy.

So they created a simple game: "1 to 5, how much do you care?" played like rock, paper, scissors.

"On three, 1 2 3, we're going to hit, you know, I'm a three, you're a four. All right, let's go your way on this."

The genius is that it exposes what passion alone can't.

You can never tell from an argument how much someone actually cares:

"Sometimes somebody will be like really passionately arguing for something... and then you're like, they're a two out of five. They just love to engage in debate."

So Brian added an built-in accountability layer:

Whoever won the decision also owned the outcome:

"You care more. Let's go your way, but if it breaks, it's on you to fix it."

When asked what happens if both people are a five out of five, Brian says it essentially never happened once. But if it did, they'd simply flip a coin.

The result?

Faster decisions, no resentment, and conviction paired with responsibility.

Rockefeller was a ruthless competitor.

Several Cleveland refiners claimed that Rockefeller had directly threatened them.

One refiner told Rockefeller he wasn't afraid of him to which Rockefeller replied:

“You may not be afraid to have your hand cut off, but your body will suffer.”

And this is the way Rockefeller did this:

You start at the top. Focus on your fiercest competitor.

Rockefeller made a list of the top refiners. He started at the top and worked his way down the list.

By the time he was half-way down the list the rest had no choice but to sell out.

Some tried to hold on and figured they could survive by expanding. But when they went to the banks to borrow money to expand they found all the bankers were already in Rockefeller's pocket.

Rockefeller was a combination of ruthless efficiency and hyper competence.

Larry Ellison is the most focused person I've ever seen when he has something to beat.

Larry has to have an enemy.

One of the biggest enemies he ever picks is Bill Gates.

This was brilliant positioning.

This is how he got Oracle in the media:

Everybody at the time was scared of Microsoft. They'd compare Microsoft to a dangerous alligator.

They'd say:

"What if we avoid the alligator?
What if we're nice to the alligator?"

This is what Larry said instead:

"Well, I've got a better idea. Let's kill the fucking alligator before he kills us! If we fight back, maybe we'll survive. Maybe we won't kill the alligator, it's a huge fucking alligator, but trying to kill it will improve our chances for survival. Being nice to the alligator will never work."

Ellison had set out to stop people talking about Oracle and other database companies, and get them talking about Oracle and Microsoft.

[As a result of his fight with Bill Gates] Oracle was now perceived as a software heavyweight.

Customers who bought our products could trust that we were going to be around for a long time.

We were a survivor.

And if customers don't believe you're going to survive — you won't

How the founder of Rolex turned the wristwatch into a status symbol and fashion piece:

"He saw an opportunity. At the time, pocket watches were passed down from father to son. They were also hidden in your pocket.

Well, you're gonna buy one pocket watch and it's gonna last for a hundred years.

But now if I take that product that was hidden in your coat and I put it on your wrist, what happens?

It becomes a fashion accessory.

People see it. It helps the product spread."

And so he said:

“The wristwatch is the type of product of which each individual likes to have not only one, but several.”

He was able to get years ahead of other watch manufacturers who persisted in clinging to the pocket watch as their chief product.

My notes from reading Poor Charlie's Almanack: The Wit and Wisdom of Charlie Munger:

1. Find a simple idea and take it seriously.

2. Good ideas are rare. When you find one bet heavily.

3. Humans have been writing down their best ideas for 5,000 years. Read them.

4. Avoiding stupid mistakes is more important than being smart.

5. Don't work with anyone you don't admire.

6. Don't sell anything you wouldn't buy.

7. Avoiding a bad habit is easier than breaking a bad habit.

8. Work on your best idea. Don't diversify

9. Incentives rule everything around you. Look for them.

10. Great businesses are built by going ridiculously far in maximizing or minimizing one or a few things. Think Costco.

11. Learning is changing behavior.

12. Do the unpleasant tasks first.

13. Charlie has read hundreds of biographies. Do the same.

14. Stop multitasking. Concentrate.

15. Many hard problems are solved best when approached backwards.

16. Think of ideas as tools. When a better tool comes along use it.

17. Clip your business and personal expenses. Small leaks sink big ships.

18. Make friends with smart dead people. Adam Smith, Darwin, Cicero, Ben Franklin —whoever interests you. Read their writing. Steal their ideas. They don't need them anymore.

19. Don't confuse intelligence with invincibility.

20. Bad things will happen to you. It's inevitable. When they do get up and keep going and remember the next maxim.

21. Self pity has no utility.

22. Find out what you are best at. Then pound away at it. Forever.

23. Only plays games where you have an edge.

24. Avoid mob rule. Avoid demagogues. Avoid dogma. Avoid bureaucracy.

25. Optimize for independence.

25. Use money to buy freedom.

26. Develop durability.

27. What do you have an *intense* interest in? Do that for money.

28. Self improvement has no end.

Jensen insists that all Nvidia employees work at the "Speed of Light."

He wants their work to be contained only by the laws of physics.

Each project must be broken down into its component tasks, and each task must have a target time-to-completion that assumes no delays, queues, or downtime.

This sets the theoretical maximum: the "Speed of Light" that it is physically impossible to exceed.

Jensen would reprimand subordinates who set goals that referred to what the company had already done before or what the competitors were doing in that moment.

As he saw it, he needed to prevent the kind of internal rot that he observed at other companies.

We will judge ourselves against the "speed of light."

Not what we used to do or what other companies are doing.
